text: Nearly every SIEM, EDR, and threat-intel platform you've touched in this path exposes a REST API, and Python's requests library is the standard way to call one. This lesson covers three patterns that separate a demo script from one safe to run unattended: OAuth2 authentication, pagination, and rate limits. Three habits to build in immediately: always pass a timeout, always check for a successful response, and always parse with dot json rather than string-slicing.

Most security platform APIs don't accept a username and password -- they use OAuth2's client credentials grant, built for one application authenticating to another with no human user involved. You register an app and get a client ID and secret; your script trades those for a short-lived access token by posting to a token endpoint with grant_type set to client_credentials. That token typically expires in seconds, so production scripts cache it and request a fresh one only when it's close to running out.

Security APIs almost never return everything in one response. A request for all indicators might return the first hundred records plus a token pointing to the next page -- the field name varies by vendor, but the pattern is the same: loop, following that token, until the API says there isn't one. This guards against a script that calls the endpoint once, gets back a fraction of the data, and quietly treats that as everything.

Every production API enforces a rate limit, and exceeding it returns an HTTP 429 response, often with a Retry-After header telling you how long to wait. A script that ignores 429s and keeps hammering the endpoint risks getting its API key throttled further or revoked. The fix is exponential backoff: wait, retry, and if it fails again, wait longer -- respecting Retry-After when given, and doubling your own delay otherwise.

Notice the habits repeated across all these examples: a timeout on every request so nothing hangs forever, raise_for_status so a failure is never silently ignored, and a token cached until genuinely close to expiring. These are the ordinary defensive habits that separate a script that survives contact with a real, rate-limited production API from one that breaks the first rough week it runs.

A real integration script combines all three pieces at once: get and cache an OAuth2 token, page through results until there's no next-page token left, and wrap every request in backoff logic that respects 429 responses. That combination, not any single piece alone, makes a script safe to run unattended. You've now covered log parsing, the STIX and TAXII data model, and REST API patterns -- the building blocks for every script ahead.
